extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evidentiary criteria for determining whether pre‑filing commercial activity or public use bars patentability under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) (and related AIA guidance). Focuses on what constitutes a sale/offer for sale, when an invention is "ready for patenting," experimental-use exceptions, territorial limits, and indicia of commercial exploitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impermissible sale/on-sale bar
rubrics_metrics.description: An impermissible sale has occurred if there was a definite sale, or offer to sell, more than 1 year before the effective filing date of the claimed invention and the subject matter of the sale, or offer to sell, fully anticipated the claimed invention or would have rendered the claimed invention obvious by its addition to the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Ferag AG v. Quipp and Pfaff: on‑sale bar triggered when (1) subject of a commercial offer for sale not primarily for experimental purposes and (2) ready for patenting. Traditional contract law and UCC principles apply to determine whether a commercial offer for sale has occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pfaff two‑prong test (on‑sale)
rubrics_metrics.description: [Pfaff v. Wells] The on‑sale bar applies when two conditions are satisfied before the critical date: (1) the product must be the subject of a commercial offer for sale (not primarily for experimental purposes); and (2) the invention must be ready for patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Pfaff to analyze both on‑sale and public‑use bars; readiness can be shown by reduction to practice or sufficiently specific drawings/descriptions enabling a skilled person to practice the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'sale' (contract/titles/UCC)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sale is a contract wherein the seller agrees to pass rights of property in return for payment or promise to pay. A contract for sale requires a concrete offer and acceptance; courts look to UCC §2-106 to define 'sale' and passage of title is a helpful indicator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: an order acknowledgment reading 'will advise-not booked' may show no acceptance. Medicines Co. v. Hospira: contract manufacturer selling services without transfer of title/right to market did not constitute invalidating sale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional sale may bar patent
rubrics_metrics.description: A sale may be deemed 'on sale' even though conditioned on buyer satisfaction; conditioning alone does not prove the sale was for experimental purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong v. General Elec. — fact of buyer satisfaction condition doesn't, without more, make transaction experimental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonprofit sale may bar patent
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'sale' need not be for profit to bar a patent; if the sale was for commercial exploitation of the invention, it is 'on sale' within the meaning of §102(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Dybel — lack of profit does not negate commercial exploitation purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single sale or offer to sell may bar patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Even a single sale or offer to sell the invention may bar patentability under §102(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consolidated Fruit‑Jar Co. v. Wright; do not require multiple transactions to find an on‑sale bar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale of rights vs sale of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment or sale of rights in the invention or potential patent rights is not, by itself, a sale of 'the invention' within the meaning of §102(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish licenses/assignments that transfer marketable product or title from those that merely grant marketing or patent rights. Examples/cases: Moleculon Research, Elan v. Andrx, In re Kollar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract manufacturing/service sale may not be on‑sale
rubrics_metrics.description: A contract manufacturer's sale of manufacturing services to an inventor (where neither title to embodiments nor right to market passes to the supplier) does not necessarily constitute a 'commercial sale' of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Medicines Co. v. Hospira: commercial benefit to parties is insufficient; transaction must be one where the product is 'commercially marketed' and title/market rights transfer is relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Buyer must be uncontrolled by seller
rubrics_metrics.description: A sale or offer for sale must take place between separate entities; if the parties are related, bar depends on whether seller so controls purchaser that the invention remains out of the public's hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Caveney; Ferag AG v. Quipp — parent/subsidiary sales may not bar if purchaser has 'essentially unfettered' management authority; assess control objectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial offer for sale — contract‑sense offer
rubrics_metrics.description: Only an offer that could be made into a binding contract by simple acceptance (assuming consideration) constitutes an offer for sale under §102(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group One: assess whether communications rise to definite commercial offer; material terms and intent to be bound matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejected or unreceived offers suffice
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere offer to sell is sufficient to bar a patent; even a rejected offer or one not actually received may create an on‑sale bar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Theis; UMC Elecs.; Wende v. Horine — do not require acceptance or receipt by purchaser.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delivery not required for on‑sale bar
rubrics_metrics.description: The on‑sale bar can apply even if the sale is not consummated and no delivery occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Buildex v. Kason; Weatherchem — signed purchase agreements prior to critical date can constitute commercial offers even if delivery/money exchange occurs after critical date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goods need not be on hand when offer made
rubrics_metrics.description: Goods need not be physically on hand and transferred at time of sale/offer; date of offer is effective date of on‑sale activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: J. A. La Porte; but the invention must be complete and 'ready for patenting' before the critical date (see Pfaff and MPEP §2133.03(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Material terms must be present in offer
rubrics_metrics.description: A communication that lacks a definite offer with material terms (price, quantities, time/place of delivery, product specifications) is not an 'offer' in the contract sense for §102(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elan v. Andrx — letters lacking material terms (e.g., asking for a licensing fee) may not be offers to sell the product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale activity need not be public
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Public' in §102(b) modifies 'use' only; sale activity does not have to be public to create an on‑sale bar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbs v. United States; AIA §102(a)(1) uses same 'on sale' term as pre‑AIA §102(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor's consent not required for third‑party sale to be prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: If a third party obtains the invention from the inventor and places it on sale more than one year before the applicant's filing date, the patent may be barred even if inventor did not consent or know of the sale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electric Storage Battery Co. v. Shimadzu; In re Blaisdell; CTS Corp. v. Electro Materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective evidence controls whether sale/offer occurred
rubrics_metrics.description: Key question: did the inventor sell or offer for sale a product that embodies the claimed invention? Objective evidence (contract descriptions, communications, drawings) controls over uncommunicated seller intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ferag AG v. Quipp: purchaser need not know of invention; any relevant evidence (correspondence, memoranda, drawings, witness testimony) may establish that offered product is the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sales by independent third parties as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: A sale or offer for sale by an independent third party more than one year before the effective filing date may be applied as prior art; exception if a patented method is kept secret after a sale by another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Caveney; consider whether sale disclosed the inventive method/structure to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non‑prior‑art publications as evidence of sale
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstracts or publications that identify a product vendor and provide buyer‑useful information (contact, price, release/installation dates) before applicant's critical date may be evidence of a sale prior to the critical date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such evidence to establish dates of release/installation that can support a rejection based on sale before the critical date (see In re Epstein example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ready for patenting — two routes
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Ready for patenting' may be satisfied either by (a) proof of reduction to practice before the critical date, or (b) proof that prior to the critical date the inventor had prepared drawings or other descriptions sufficiently specific to enable a person skilled in the art to practice the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pfaff; Invitrogen; examples where detailed drawings/specs allowed manufacture of claimed product. Readiness is applied in both on‑sale and public‑use contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to practice before sale triggers bar
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention was actually reduced to practice before being sold or offered for sale more than one year before filing, patentability is barred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vanmoor v. Wal‑Mart: completed products made to unchanged specifications before critical date show reduction to practice; testing under working conditions typically required to show practical utility unless invention is self‑evidently operative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherent possession of claim limitations in offered product
rubrics_metrics.description: If a product offered for sale inherently possesses each limitation of the claims, then the invention is on sale, whether or not parties recognized the claimed characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abbott Labs v. Geneva Pharmaceuticals; STX LLC v. Brine Inc. — subjective unknown qualities cannot avoid the on‑sale bar.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 CFR 1.131 affidavits/declarations may admit earlier completion
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits/declarations under 37 C.F.R. 1.131 submitted to swear behind a reference may themselves constitute admissions that an invention was 'complete' more than one year before filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Foster; Dart Indus. — examine such statements carefully; see MPEP §715.10 for guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale of a process — know‑how vs carried‑out process
rubrics_metrics.description: Sale of 'know‑how' describing a process (without the process being carried out) is not a 'sale' of the claimed process within the meaning of §102(b); sale of a product made by the claimed process, or sale/offer to perform the process, can trigger §102(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Kollar; D.L. Auld Co.; Scaltech v. Retec/Tetra — sale of device embodying the process or sale of the product made by the process can bar method claims. Assess whether the device was used to practice the claimed method before critical date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territoriality — 'in this country' requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: For pre‑AIA §102(b) purposes, 'in this country' includes any U.S. State, D.C., and U.S. commonwealths/territories/possessions; public use or on‑sale activity must take place in the United States to trigger the bar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign manufacture/delivery generally does not trigger on‑sale bar, but substantial prefatory activity in the U.S., or offers originating/communicated to the U.S., may suffice (CTS Corp. v. Piher Int’l). See 35 U.S.C. 105 and relevant cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental use doctrine — primary purpose test
rubrics_metrics.description: A use or sale is experimental (and thus may be permitted) if the primary purpose of the inventor at the time of the sale was to conduct experimentation — a bona fide effort to perfect the invention or to ascertain whether it will answer its intended purpose; any commercial exploitation must be merely incidental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allen Eng'g v. Bartell; LaBounty v. United States Int'l Trade Comm'n; Pennwalt v. Akzona. Market testing to gauge consumer demand is not experimental (In re Smith).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial exploitation policy limit
rubrics_metrics.description: One policy of the on‑sale/public‑use provisions is to prevent inventors from commercially exploiting inventions more than one year prior to filing; even bona fide experimental activity cannot be used to commercially exploit the invention beyond the grace period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Theis: if precritical activity is an attempt at market penetration, it may be cited as prior art despite claimed experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial activity must legitimately advance development
rubrics_metrics.description: The commercial activity (sale/use) must legitimately advance the experimental development of the invention toward completion; otherwise it counts as commercial exploitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where examiner finds prima facie sale/offer, applicant rarely meets burden to show experimentation unless clear and convincing necessity for the experimentation is established. See Sunoco Partners Marketing & Terminals LP v. U.S. Venture — testing at third party location and ability to test earlier undermined experimental claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicia of commercial exploitation (factors A–F)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective activities indicative of commercial exploitation include: (A) preparation of contemporaneous commercial documents (orders, invoices, receipts, delivery schedules); (B) preparation/distribution of price lists and quotations; (C) display of samples to prospective customers; (D) demonstration of models/prototypes (especially at trade conventions); (E) use where an admission fee is charged; (F) advertising/publicity, brochures, periodical notices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these as indicia of subjective intent to commercially exploit. See cases cited (Akron Brass, Amphenol, Cataphote, Monogram, General Elec., Red Cross Mfg., In re Theis, Interroyal Corp., Tucker Aluminum). See also MPEP §2133.03(e)(4) for experimental‑purpose factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent — requirement for objective evidence of experimental purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: When sales occur in an ordinary commercial environment and goods are placed outside inventor's control, a secretly held subjective intent to 'experiment' is unavailing without objective evidence; under such circumstances the customer must, at a minimum, be made aware of the intended experimental purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether objective evidence supports claimed experimental intent; mere subjective assertions are insufficient when transaction is commercial in nature.
